subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]
passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the bus shelter outside the nursery school, and the van was late. Hemant's tiffin had slipped from his hands into a puddle, and now he was crying, big shaky sobs. Raghav looked into his own pocket. Only one biscuit left, a bit squashed. He looked at it for a long moment. Then he snapped it in two and held out the bigger half. "Here. Don't cry." He patted Hemant's wet sleeve, pat, pat, pat, the way Amma pats him at night. Hemant took the biscuit and hiccuped. The two boys ate slowly, shoulders touching, watching for the van.

qa.q: What fell into the puddle?
qa.a: Hemant's tiffin slipped from his hands into a puddle.

qa.q: What does Raghav looking at the biscuit for a long moment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted it for himself too, but his care for his crying friend won, so he shared the bigger half.

qa.q: What could a teacher say to Raghav the next day to encourage this?
qa.a: The teacher could tell Raghav they noticed how he shared and patted Hemant, and ask how he thought Hemant felt afterwards.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Hemant after Raghav shared?
qa.a: Hemant went from sobbing alone to eating with a friend, shoulders touching, so the wet, late wait felt safer and less lonely.

grounding: A young child breaks his last biscuit to share with a crying friend and pats him, kindness flowing from closeness.

subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]
passage: Gautam's red balloon popped on the gate of their building, and he burst into tears so loud that the watchman looked over. Jaya ran across the courtyard with her packet of cream biscuits. She pulled one out, broke it carefully, and pushed half into Gautam's hand. "You can have the one with more cream." Gautam kept crying. Jaya stood close and patted his back with her small flat hand. "Tomorrow my Papa will buy two balloons. One for you." Gautam wiped his nose on his sleeve and took a bite. Jaya smiled and ate her half, the one with less cream.

qa.q: Where did Gautam's balloon pop?
qa.a: On the gate of their building.

qa.q: Why did Jaya give Gautam the half with more cream?
qa.a: She wanted to cheer up her crying friend and felt so much for him that she gave him the better half.

qa.q: What worked when Gautam kept crying, and why?
qa.a: Jaya stayed close, patted his back and promised a new balloon, so he felt comforted enough to take a bite.

qa.q: How might the watchman see what Jaya did?
qa.a: The watchman, who heard the loud crying, might be touched to see a little girl run over and share her biscuit to comfort a friend 🙂

grounding: A young girl shares her biscuit with a crying friend and pats him, showing early kindness toward someone close.

subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]
passage: "Why are you crying?" Usha asked. Imran sat on the school steps, knees up. "Ammi's late. Everybody's gone." "My Nani's late too." Usha sat beside him. "Are you hungry?" He shook his head, then nodded. Usha opened her tiffin. One biscuit left. She broke it. "Half for you." "It's yours." "Friends share. Take it." Imran took it. Usha patted his arm. "Your Ammi always comes. Remember last time? She came running with an umbrella." Imran gave a tiny laugh. "She was all wet." "Like a duck," said Usha. They were both giggling when the gate opened.

qa.q: How many biscuits were left in Usha's tiffin?
qa.a: One biscuit left.

qa.q: How was Imran feeling on the school steps?
qa.a: He felt scared and lonely because his Ammi was late and everyone had gone.

qa.q: Which choice by Usha turned Imran's tears into giggles?
qa.a: Usha shared her last biscuit and reminded him of the funny umbrella day, giving him comfort and a reason to laugh.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had just waited on her own?
qa.a: Imran would likely have kept crying alone, feeling that nobody cared, and the wait would have felt much longer for him.

grounding: At the school steps a young child shares her last biscuit with a crying friend and pats his arm, showing early kindness.

passage: I'm Sarika, Irawati's older sister. I'm in the same school, so I saw it all last week. Megha, Irawati's best friend, came to class with a fever and her mother came to fetch her at lunch. Irawati picked up Megha's heavy bag as well as her own and carried both down three floors, red in the face. The next day some girls crowded around Irawati asking why Megha had been crying in the corridor before the fever. Irawati just said, "She wasn't feeling well." I found out later Megha had told Irawati something private about her grandmother's dog dying. Irawati never told anyone, not even me. I don't know what she was thinking, but she looked very serious about it.

qa.q: How many floors did Irawati carry both bags down?
qa.a: Three floors.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling when the girls crowded around asking questions?
qa.a: She probably felt protective of Megha and determined to keep her trust, which is why she gave only a short answer and looked serious.

qa.q: What choice at the corridor showed Irawati's loyalty?
qa.a: When the girls asked why Megha was crying, Irawati chose to say only that Megha wasn't feeling well, keeping the private news safe.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Irawati's silence?
qa.a: Sarika isn't sure what Irawati was thinking, but seems impressed that Irawati kept the secret even from her own sister.

grounding: An older sister observes a child carrying a sick friend's bag and keeping a harmless secret she was trusted with.

passage: Monday: At recess, Aditi whispered to Zainab behind the water tank, "We're moving to Bhopal next month. Don't tell anyone yet, I want to tell them myself." Zainab crossed her heart. Wednesday: Aditi came to school with a bad cold and a thick scarf. Zainab carried Aditi's bag up to the classroom and back down at home time, even though her own was heavy with atlases. When Ritika asked, "Why is Aditi so quiet lately? Is something wrong?" Zainab shrugged and changed the subject to the cricket match. Friday: Aditi stood up in class and told everyone about moving. Afterwards she hugged Zainab hard. "You didn't tell. Not even Ritika." Zainab grinned. "It was yours to tell."

qa.q: Where are Aditi's family moving?
qa.a: To Bhopal, next month.

qa.q: Why did Zainab change the subject when Ritika asked about Aditi?
qa.a: Zainab wanted to protect Aditi's trust and let Aditi share the news in her own way.

qa.q: What choices across the week showed Zainab's loyalty?
qa.a: Zainab carried Aditi's bag while she was ill and kept the moving news secret until Aditi told everyone herself.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel toward Zainab by Friday?
qa.a: Aditi feels grateful and close to Zainab, hugging her hard because the secret was kept 🤗

grounding: Over a week a child carries an ill friend's bag and keeps her friend's secret until the friend chooses to share it.

passage: Ojas, you want a story? When I was ten, my best friend Bansi got jaundice and was weak for weeks. Our school was two kilometres away, over the canal bridge. Every morning I walked to his house first, took his cloth bag, and carried both of ours. My shoulders ached. My mother said, "Harish, you're not his coolie." I didn't care. Bansi was mine to look after. There was something else too. Bansi couldn't read the blackboard well yet, and he was ashamed. He asked me to whisper the words to him, and not to tell. I whispered for a whole year. I never told the teacher or the other boys. You're the first person I've told, and Bansi is ninety now, so I think he'll forgive me.

qa.q: How far away was the school?
qa.a: Two kilometres away, over the canal bridge.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about carrying both bags despite aching shoulders?
qa.a: Harish felt that Bansi was his to look after, so caring for his friend mattered more than the ache or his mother's teasing.

qa.q: What was the key choice Harish made about Bansi's reading, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Harish chose to whisper the words and keep it secret, which protected Bansi from shame while still helping him learn.

qa.q: What was it like for Bansi to have a friend like Harish?
qa.a: Bansi, weak and ashamed, had someone to carry his bag and quietly help him read, so he could keep going to school without being mocked.

grounding: An elder recalls carrying a sick friend's bag as a boy and keeping the friend's harmless secret out of loyalty.

passage: The power went out at nine, the night before Uday's first semester exam in Pune. He sat in the dark with his phone at four per cent, having just hung up on his mother in Guwahati. Her voice had made the flat feel even further from home. He hadn't told anyone he was homesick. Then there was a knock. Harsha, his flatmate, stood holding a candle and two steel tumblers of ginger tea. "Thought you might want this." Harsha didn't ask anything, just sat on the floor and started talking about the mess food. Uday laughed for the first time that day. When the lights came back an hour later, neither of them got up. Uday thought: this is someone I can count on.

qa.q: What did Harsha bring to Uday's room?
qa.a: A candle and two steel tumblers of ginger tea.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after hanging up on his mother?
qa.a: He felt homesick and lonely, as if the flat was even further from home.

qa.q: What was the turning point of Uday's night, and why did it help?
qa.a: Harsha's unasked visit with tea and easy talk turned a lonely evening into company, showing Uday he could count on someone here.

qa.q: What might Harsha have noticed that led to the knock?
qa.a: Harsha may have noticed Uday seemed low or heard the phone call end, and chose to offer company quietly without asking questions.

grounding: A homesick student receives tea and company from a flatmate without asking, and feels he belongs.

passage: It was Devika's third week in the Mumbai paying-guest flat, and Sunday was the worst day. At home in Mysuru, Sunday meant Amma's rasam, cousins, noise. Here there was just the fan and her laptop. She didn't cry; she just lay very still. Around four, Manjula, the flatmate she barely knew, tapped on the door with a tray: two cups of tea and a plate of hot bajji from the corner stall. "I saw you skipped lunch. Want to watch something silly?" They watched an old comedy on Manjula's laptop, knees up on the bed. Manjula didn't make a speech. She just came again next Sunday, and the one after. By the third week, Devika left her own door open on Sundays.

qa.q: What was on Manjula's tray?
qa.a: Two cups of tea and a plate of hot bajji from the corner stall.

qa.q: What does Devika lying very still suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and homesick, missing the noise and warmth of Sundays at home.

qa.q: What made Manjula's kindness so powerful for Devika?
qa.a: It came without being asked and kept coming every Sunday, so Devika learned she could rely on it and slowly opened her own door.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had only visited once?
qa.a: Devika might have felt a moment of comfort but not the steady sense of belonging that repeated Sundays gave her.

grounding: A homesick young woman is brought tea and time by a flatmate without asking and gradually feels she belongs.

passage: "You've been sitting on these steps for an hour." Chaitanya looked up. Pradeep, from the room next door in the hostel block, stood there holding two paper cups of canteen chai. "How did you know?" "Saw you from the window. Here." Chaitanya took the cup. "My grandmother called. Everyone's at home for the festival. I'm just... here." "Yeah." Pradeep sat down one step below. "Want to talk?" "Not really." "Okay." They drank. A crow hopped near. "Same time tomorrow?" Pradeep asked. Chaitanya looked at him. "You'd come again?" "Every day of the festival, if you want." Chaitanya felt something in his chest unknot. "Yeah. I'd like that."

qa.q: What was Pradeep holding when he came to the steps?
qa.a: Two paper cups of canteen chai.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya feel when his chest unknots?
qa.a: He feels relief and safety, sensing that someone cares about him while he is away from home during the festival.

qa.q: What choice made Pradeep's kindness work so well?
qa.a: Pradeep brought chai without being asked and accepted 'not really' without pushing, then offered to come every day, which made the care feel dependable.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's grandmother feel if she knew about Pradeep?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and comforted that someone was looking out for her grandson while the family celebrated without him.

grounding: A homesick student on the hostel steps receives unasked chai and quiet company from a fellow student and feels he belongs.

passage: Sarika, you're doing it again, saying yes to everyone. Sit, I'll tell you what happened to your Lavanya Mami at your age. At twenty-five I cooked for my in-laws, tutored my cousin's son, ran my friends' errands and worked full-time at the bank. Everyone called me the helpful one. I liked it. Then one night at a wedding I fainted, just from being empty. The doctor said I needed rest. Lying there, I understood: if I break, nobody gets help from me at all. So I learned a small word. No. "No, not this Sunday." "No, I can't tutor this month, but here's a friend who can." I still help, beta. Just not until I'm hollow. Now, drink this, and tell your manager no.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya faint?
qa.a: At a wedding.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel about being called the helpful one, before the fainting?
qa.a: Lavanya liked being called the helpful one and enjoyed it, which made it harder to notice how empty she was getting.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lavanya, and what changed afterwards?
qa.a: Fainting at the wedding showed that if she broke, nobody would be helped, so she started saying no sometimes while still helping.

qa.q: How might Sarika hear this story from Lavanya Mami?
qa.a: Sarika may feel understood and gently warned, seeing that saying no to a manager doesn't mean Sarika stops being kind.

grounding: An elder recalls learning in her twenties to say no when exhausted so that her generous help could last.

passage: Yogesh had worked double shifts at the hospital lab all week, and his eyes felt full of sand. On Saturday night, as rain hammered the window, Dhruv called. "Bro, can you help me shift flats tomorrow? Six a.m. The truck's booked." Yogesh always said yes. He'd helped Dhruv move twice already, and fixed his mother's fan last month. He opened his mouth to say yes again, then felt how heavy his arms were. "Dhruv, I can't tomorrow. I'm wrecked. If I carry your fridge like this, I'll drop it on my foot." Silence. "But I'll come Wednesday evening and help you unpack and set up the kitchen. Promise." Dhruv sighed, then laughed. "Fine. Bring the good screwdriver." Yogesh slept eleven hours.

qa.q: How long did Yogesh sleep after the call?
qa.a: Yogesh slept eleven hours.

qa.q: What made Yogesh hesitate before saying yes again?
qa.a: He felt how heavy his arms were and how exhausted he was, and worried he could not help safely in that state.

qa.q: Which choice kept Yogesh both kind and rested?
qa.a: He said no to Sunday but offered Wednesday evening for unpacking, which protected his rest while still showing he cared.

qa.q: How does Dhruv seem to take Yogesh's no?
qa.a: Dhruv is a bit disappointed at first, shown by the silence and sigh, but accepts it with a laugh because help is still coming.

grounding: A generous young man, exhausted after double shifts, says no to a friend's request while offering help at a better time.

passage: For a month Sabina had cooked lunch for her uncle's family after his surgery, dropped her nieces to tuition and answered every call from her office at night. On Thursday her brother Bhupen came to her Kolkata flat with a cardboard box. "The kids have a science model due Monday. You're so good at these." Sabina looked at the box, then at the clock: nine-forty. Her head throbbed. "Bhupen, I love them. I'll help on Sunday for one hour, to show them how. But I won't make it for them, and not tonight." He blinked. "You never say no." "I know. That's the problem." After he left, she made tea, sat on the balcony and watched the tram lights pass. She felt guilty for ten minutes. Then she felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring to Sabina's flat?
qa.a: A cardboard box for the kids' science model.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after Bhupen left?
qa.a: She felt guilty for ten minutes, and then she felt lighter.

qa.q: What was the key choice Sabina made with Bhupen, and why was it balanced?
qa.a: She offered one hour on Sunday to show the children how, but refused to build the model herself that night, protecting her energy while still helping.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see his sister after she says no?
qa.a: Bhupen is surprised because she never refused before, but he may start to notice how much she has been carrying.

grounding: An adult who has been helping her family generously says no to one more request when exhausted, still offering limited help.

passage: Recess was only ten minutes today because of the assembly, and Akash was picking the kho-kho team fast. "You, you, you." He skipped right past Tsering, the new boy whose family had come from Darjeeling. "Not him, he talks funny." A few kids laughed. Aparna felt her face go hot. Tsering looked down at his shoes. There were only seven minutes left. Aparna could have just played. Instead she said loudly, "That's not fair. He runs faster than you, Akash. And how he talks has nothing to do with kho-kho." Akash rolled his eyes. "Fine, take him then." Aparna pulled Tsering onto her side. He tagged three people before the bell. On the way back in, he walked next to her.

qa.q: Where had Tsering's family come from?
qa.a: From Darjeeling.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when Akash said Tsering talks funny?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed for Tsering, her face going hot, because leaving him out was unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna face, and why did her choice matter?
qa.a: With only seven minutes left she could have just played, but she chose to speak up, which got Tsering into the game and showed fairness is for everyone.

qa.q: How might Tsering have felt when he walked back next to Aparna?
qa.a: Tsering probably felt relieved and welcome, after first looking down at his shoes when he was left out.

grounding: A child objects when a classmate from another community is left out of a game, showing fairness beyond her friends.

passage: Every evening the boys and girls of Sunrise Apartments played cricket in the parking lot. Bablu, whose family lived in the construction workers' sheds behind the building, watched from the wall. Today he asked, "Can I bat?" Arnab, who owned the bat, said, "This is only for building kids." Gopika, eleven, was fielding at point. She thought of her cousin who had moved to a new city and cried because no one let her play. She walked in. "Arnab, that's a rubbish rule. He's a kid. The lot is big enough." "My bat, my rule." "Then I'm not playing either." Two others dropped their gloves too. Arnab scowled, then held out the bat. Bablu hit the first ball over the gate.

qa.q: Where did the children play cricket every evening?
qa.a: In the parking lot of Sunrise Apartments.

qa.q: Why did Gopika think of her cousin when Bablu was refused?
qa.a: She remembered how hurt her cousin felt when left out in a new city, which made her feel strongly that Bablu deserved a turn too.

qa.q: Which choice changed Arnab's mind, and why did it work?
qa.a: Gopika refused to play unless Bablu could, and others followed, so Arnab saw the rule was unfair and not worth losing the game over.

qa.q: How might Bablu have felt watching from the wall each day?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and wishful, wanting to join but unsure if he was welcome, until today when he finally asked.

grounding: A child stands up for a boy from a different community who is excluded from a game, calling it unfair.

passage: "She can't play, she doesn't even understand Tamil," Manoj said, holding the ball. Dhruv looked at the girl standing by the school tap. Kiran had joined last week from Lucknow. "So? We can say the rules in English. Or show her." "It'll be slow." "It won't. Kiran, want to play?" Kiran nodded, cautious. Manoj crossed his arms. "Why do you care? She's not our friend." "Because it's not fair," Dhruv said. "She's in our class. If I went to Lucknow, I'd want someone to let me play." Manoj kicked at the dust. "Fine. But you explain." Dhruv held up two fingers. "Two bounces, then catch." Kiran grinned and caught the next throw clean.

qa.q: Where had Kiran joined from?
qa.a: From Lucknow.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv care about Kiran joining, even though she isn't his friend?
qa.a: He believes it is unfair to leave her out and imagines how he would want to be treated in a new place.

qa.q: What choice made including Kiran work in practice?
qa.a: Dhruv explained the rules with simple gestures and words, so the game didn't slow down and Kiran could join in easily.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt when Manoj said she couldn't play?
qa.a: Kiran probably felt nervous and left out as a new student, which is why she nodded cautiously before grinning when she caught the ball.

grounding: A child insists that a new classmate from another state be included in the game because excluding her is unfair.

passage: Monday: Gopika couldn't sleep. The news had shown whole villages in a far-off state under brown water, a girl her age carrying a goat on her shoulders. "Why do we just watch?" she asked her mother, Sangeeta, angry and close to tears. Wednesday: The school eco club had a tree-planting drive on the bare hillside behind the stadium. The forest officer explained how roots hold soil so rain doesn't rush down all at once. Gopika dug three holes, her hands blistered, and felt the knot in her stomach loosen a little. Saturday: She set up a collection box outside the canteen for flood relief, with a sign she'd painted herself. "It's small," she told Sangeeta. "But it's something."

qa.q: How many holes did Gopika dig?
qa.a: Gopika dug three holes.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she asked, 'Why do we just watch?'
qa.a: She felt angry and upset, overwhelmed by the suffering of people far away and frustrated at feeling helpless.

qa.q: What turning point helped Gopika turn worry into action?
qa.a: Learning from the forest officer how roots hold soil made her see a link to the floods, and she acted by planting and then setting up a collection box.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see her daughter's week?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel worried at first by Gopika's distress but proud to see it turn into planting trees and a relief box.

grounding: Across a week a teenager worries about far-away flood victims, joins a tree planting and starts a relief box, as she grasps how the world is linked.

passage: Sumit, sit. You asked why I plant a tree every monsoon. When I was fifteen, the river near our town flooded the villages downstream. We were safe on the hill. But I saw the boats bringing people with nothing, children wrapped in sacks. I couldn't eat for two days. I kept asking why. Our science teacher took us up the ghat and showed us the stumps where the forest had been cut. "Rain runs off bare slopes like off a roof," she said. That Sunday I went with the college boys to plant saplings, the only girl in the group. My hands bled. Some saplings died. But I kept going every year. Your Urmila Dadi has planted fifty-eight trees. And I still think about those children.

qa.q: How old was Urmila when the river flooded the villages downstream?
qa.a: Fifteen.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel after seeing the boats bring people with nothing?
qa.a: She was so upset she couldn't eat for two days and kept asking why, showing deep concern for strangers she had never met.

qa.q: What turning point turned Urmila's worry into action?
qa.a: The teacher showing the cut stumps on the ghat helped her see how bare slopes cause floods, and she chose to start planting saplings.

qa.q: What might Sumit take away from Urmila Dadi's story?
qa.a: Sumit might see that caring for people far away can lead to steady small actions, like planting a tree every monsoon.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenage girl, concern for flood victims downstream led her to plant trees once she understood how deforestation causes floods.

passage: The tree-planting drive started at seven, but by ten the sun was brutal and there were only forty saplings for sixty volunteers. Vijay, sixteen, wiped his face with his T-shirt. On his phone that morning he'd seen photos of a coastal town in another country, houses gone, people sleeping on a school roof. He'd felt sick and angry. What was the point of a few trees here? He said so to Sarita, the volunteer coordinator. She handed him a sapling. "Mangroves on coasts, forests on hills, all the same story. Less heat, fewer floods. Every place connected." Vijay dug slowly, thinking about that. Then he asked for her number: the school holidays were coming, and he wanted to join the mangrove drive.

qa.q: How many saplings were there for sixty volunteers?
qa.a: Only forty saplings.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after seeing the photos of the coastal town?
qa.a: He felt sick and angry, and wondered if his few trees here could make any difference.

qa.q: What turning point changed Vijay's view of his work?
qa.a: Sarita explained how forests and mangroves everywhere reduce heat and floods, so Vijay saw the connection and chose to join the mangrove drive too.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Vijay's frustrated question?
qa.a: Sarita probably sees it as real concern, not laziness, and uses it as a chance to explain how places are linked.

grounding: A teenager planting trees feels anxious about far-off flood victims and grows wider concern as he learns how the world is connected.

subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
passage: Monday: Himani was the student member on the college scholarship panel, and the shortlist landed in her inbox. Pallavi, her best friend since school, was on it. So was a student she didn't know, whose file said she worked evenings to pay rent. Only one scholarship left. Himani stared at the screen past midnight. Wednesday: She told the panel head that Pallavi was her close friend and asked to step out of that decision. "It's not fair to anyone if I vote," she said. Then she called Pallavi and told her the truth. Pallavi went quiet. Saturday: The other student got it. Pallavi came over anyway with samosas. "I was angry," she said. "But I'd have hated winning because of you."

qa.q: What did Himani ask the panel head on Wednesday?
qa.a: She asked to step out of that decision because Pallavi was her close friend.

qa.q: Why did Himani stare at the screen past midnight?
qa.a: She was torn between wanting to help her best friend and feeling it would be unfair to the other student who needed the scholarship.

qa.q: What choice helped Himani handle the conflict well?
qa.a: She declared her friendship, stepped out of the vote and told Pallavi honestly, working through the tension instead of quietly favouring her friend.

qa.q: How does Pallavi feel about Himani's choice by Saturday?
qa.a: Pallavi was angry at first, but by Saturday she understands and even says she would have hated winning unfairly.

grounding: A young woman is torn between loyalty to her best friend and fairness for all on a scholarship panel, and works through it honestly.

subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
passage: Manjula, come, sit. You asked if I ever fought with family over something right. When I was twenty-one, I kept the books for my uncle's garment workshop. He had taken me in when Papa died, and I loved him. One month I noticed the women stitching collars got less than the men stitching cuffs, same hours, same skill. I couldn't sleep. If I said nothing, I betrayed them. If I shouted, I betrayed him. So I made a list, sat with him after dinner, and showed him the numbers. He was angry. He said I was ungrateful. I came back the next week, and the next. By Diwali, the pay was the same. Your Devika Mausi still says it was the hardest winter of her life.

qa.q: What did the narrator keep the books for at twenty-one?
qa.a: For her uncle's garment workshop.

qa.q: Why couldn't Devika sleep after noticing the pay difference?
qa.a: She felt torn between her love and gratitude toward her uncle and her sense that the women workers were being treated unfairly.

qa.q: What turning point shows Devika working through the tension instead of choosing carelessly?
qa.a: Devika chose to show her uncle the numbers calmly and kept returning week after week, instead of staying silent or shouting.

qa.q: How might the women stitching collars have been affected by Devika's choice?
qa.a: They would finally be paid the same as the men for the same work, a real difference in their lives even if they never knew who pushed for it.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling torn at twenty-one between loyalty to her uncle and fairness for his workers, and working through it patiently.

subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
passage: The selection list had to reach the coach by six, and Lokesh's phone was at eight per cent. He was the student assistant timing the athletics trials. Baljeet, his best friend since class one, had run the 400 metres in 58.9. The new boy from the hostel had run 57.4. Only one place was left. At five-thirty Baljeet found him in the stand. "Just write 57. Nobody will check. You know how much I've trained." Lokesh felt sick. Baljeet had stood by him through everything. But the new boy had trained too. "I can't change a number," Lokesh said, voice shaking. "But I'll come with you now to ask Coach if there's a re-run tomorrow. That's allowed." Baljeet stared, then turned away. Lokesh sent the true list at 5.52.

qa.q: What was Baljeet's time in the 400 metres?
What was Lokesh feeling when Baljeet asked him to write 57?

subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
passage: It was forty-two degrees on election day, and the queue outside the school booth snaked round the playground. Sahil, twenty-five, had spent two evenings reading the candidates' records on the election commission's site and comparing their promises about the ward's water supply. Ahead of him, his neighbour Dolma-la, seventy and slow on the stairs, was fanning herself with a newspaper. Sahil gave her his umbrella and his water bottle, then walked her to the shade to wait until her turn came. After voting he went straight to the community kitchen near the market, where he'd volunteered every Sunday for a year. He didn't talk about big ideas much. He just kept showing up.

qa.q: What did Sahil give Dolma-la?
qa.a: His umbrella and his water bottle.

qa.q: What does Sahil spending two evenings on the candidates' records suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he takes his vote seriously and wants to choose thoughtfully for the ward, not just vote out of habit.

qa.q: Which of Sahil's choices show his values working in everyday life?
qa.a: Reading the records before voting, helping Dolma-la in the heat and volunteering every Sunday show care turned into small, steady actions.

qa.q: How might Dolma-la see Sahil?
qa.a: Dolma-la probably sees him as a kind, dependable neighbour who noticed her struggling in the heat and quietly helped.

grounding: An adult turns concern for others into steady local acts: thoughtful voting, volunteering and helping a neighbour.

passage: Every Saturday morning, Avni's small living room in the Pune flat filled with children: the watchman's two sons, the girls whose mothers cooked in the building, a boy from the Somali family on the fifth floor. Avni, twenty-four, taught them English with picture cards and bad jokes. Her flatmate Kashish watched from the kitchen door. Avni greeted the sweeper, Ramesh-bhau, by name every morning, always asked after his knee, and had signed up to help at the ward's polling booth next month. "You never post about any of this," Kashish said. Avni shrugged, sorting crayons. "It's not a speech. It's just Saturday." Kashish found herself picking up a stack of cards to help.

qa.q: What did Avni use to teach the children English?
qa.a: Picture cards and bad jokes.

qa.a: Avni doesn't see the teaching as something to show off; it feels like a normal part of her week, not a grand act.

qa.a: Kashish seems to admire her and is quietly moved to join in, picking up the cards to help.

grounding: An adult puts wide concern into action through weekly teaching, respect for neighbours from all backgrounds and civic volunteering.

You carried their gas cylinder." "They'd just moved from Manipur. They didn't know anyone." "You also read all those ward candidate lists before voting." "Somebody should." Vijay tied his shoes. "I can't fix the world, didi. I can fix our lane and say hello." Sarita sighed and reached for her chappals. "Fine. One hour. Show me this drain."

passage: The queue for the tallest water slide at the park wound up the stairs in the blazing sun, and the sign said you had to be as tall as the red line. Swati, nine, pressed her back against it, stretching her neck. Just over. "Yogesh bhaiya, please! We've done the small one four times. It's so boring." Her cousin looked up at the twisting yellow tube. "It's really fast." "That's the point!" Swati's eyes were shining. They waited forty minutes. At the top her legs shook a little. Then she pushed off and screamed the whole way down, into the pool, and came up spluttering and laughing. "Again! And then the black one!"

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: At the Dussehra fair near Pallavi's colony, her father Uday bought tickets for the merry-go-round. Pallavi, ten, sat on a painted horse for one round and climbed off. "Papa, that's for babies. The swing boat! And the dark house! And that new spinning thing!" "You haven't even finished your candy floss." "I'll eat it in the queue." She dragged him from ride to ride, eyes on every new flashing light. The spinning ride made her stomach flip and she shrieked with joy. Then she spotted a stall where you threw rings over bottles. "I've never done that one!" Uday laughed, out of breath. "Is there anything you won't try?" "Boring things," Pallavi said.

grounding: A child at a fair wants every new ride and finds the merry-go-round boring; novelty and excitement feel like life to her.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: "Ishita didi, I'm bored. Bored bored bored." "You've got a whole shelf of games, Aditi." "I've played them all. A hundred times." Aditi flopped onto her bed. "Can I ride my cycle down the steep lane? No hands?" "No hands, definitely not." "Then what? Everything is boring." Ishita thought. "Okay. New challenge. Build an obstacle course in the hall with cushions. I'll time you." Aditi sat up. "With the stool as a tunnel?" "Sure." "And if I beat two minutes, then I try the lane? With hands?" "With hands, helmet, and me watching." "Deal!" Aditi was already dragging cushions.

grounding: At home a child bored with familiar games craves a new thrill, and her sister channels it into a safer challenge.

passage: The substitute teacher had to leave the class alone for twenty minutes, and the room got loud. Amandeep sat very straight, finishing the map worksheet exactly as the instructions said. His group was making a poster on rivers, and Jatin, the group leader, drew the Ganga flowing into the Arabian Sea. Amandeep knew it was wrong. He had read it last night. He opened his mouth, then closed it. Everyone else was nodding. What if Jatin got annoyed? What if they called him a know-it-all? He coloured the river carefully the wrong way. At the end the teacher came back and said, "Who drew this? It goes to the Bay of Bengal." Amandeep stared at his crayon, cheeks burning.

qa.q: Where did Jatin draw the Ganga flowing into?
qa.a: Into the Arabian Sea.

qa.a: He was afraid Jatin would get annoyed or that the group would call him a know-it-all, so fear of disapproval kept him quiet.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try next time he knows something the group has wrong?
qa.a: He could say it gently, like 'I read it goes to the Bay of Bengal, shall we check?', which keeps the peace and still shares what he knows.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel if Amandeep had spoken up?
qa.a: Jatin might have felt a moment of surprise, but probably would have been glad to fix the poster before the teacher saw it.

grounding: A rule-following child keeps quiet about a mistake to avoid upsetting the group, burying what he knows.

passage: At home, Manoj talked in his Nani's Bhojpuri, full of jokes and funny words. At his new school in Delhi, he didn't say a single one. He copied how Siddharth and the other boys spoke, wore his socks pulled up exactly like them, and never forgot his tie. When the class teacher asked for ideas for the class trip, Manoj thought of the old stepwell near his Nani's house. He'd been there; it was amazing. But Siddharth said, "Let's just do the mall," and everyone agreed. Manoj stayed quiet. At home that night he told Nani about the stepwell in a rush of words. "Why didn't you say it in class?" she asked. Manoj shrugged. "Nobody else said anything different."

qa.a: The old stepwell near his Nani's house.

qa.a: He wants to fit in and fears standing out, since nobody else said anything different from Siddharth.

qa.a: He could tell the teacher his idea privately or bring a photo of the stepwell, so it feels less risky than speaking up in front of everyone.

qa.a: Nani knows the chatty, funny boy at home, so she may be puzzled and a little sad that he hides that side in class.

grounding: A child copies classmates' dress and speech and holds back his own idea, fitting in at the cost of his own opinion.
